message.content:
**Freezing point of water at 10 kPa**

| Pressure | Freezing point (°C) |
|----------|---------------------|
| 101.3 kPa (1 atm) | 0.00 °C |
| 10 kPa | **≈ +0.5 °C** |

---

### How that number is obtained

The melting (freezing) curve of water is described by the Clausius–Clapeyron relation:

\[
\frac{dP}{dT} \;=\; \frac{L_{\text{fus}}}{T\,\Delta V}
\]

where  

* \(L_{\text{fus}}\) ≈ 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ (latent heat of fusion)  
* \(T\) ≈ 273 K (≈ 0 °C)  
* \(\Delta V = V_{\text{ice}} - V_{\text{liquid}}\) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ m³ mol⁻¹

Plugging in gives

\[
\frac{dP}{dT} \approx \frac{6.01\times10^{3}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}}
{273\,\text{K}\times1.3\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{3}\text{mol}^{-1}}
\approx 1.69\times10^{5}\,\text{Pa K}^{-1}
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{dT}{dP} \approx \frac{1}{1.69\times10^{5}}\;\text{K Pa}^{-1}
\approx 5.9\times10^{-3}\;\text{K Pa}^{-1}
\]

A drop of pressure from 101.3 kPa to 10 kPa is a decrease of 91.3 kPa, so

\[
\Delta T \approx 5.9\times10^{-3}\,\text{K Pa}^{-1}\times 91.3\times10^{3}\,\text{Pa}
\approx 0.54\,\text{K}
\]

Adding this to the 0 °C freezing point at 1 atm gives

\[
T_{\text{freeze}}(10\,\text{kPa}) \approx 0.54\,^\circ\text{C}
\]

Rounded to one decimal place, the freezing point is **+0.5 °C**.

---

### Practical note

At 10 kPa (≈ 0.1 atm), water will freeze at a temperature slightly above 0 °C, roughly +0.5 °C. This is why, for example, water can remain liquid at temperatures just below 0 °C when the pressure is reduced (e.g., in a vacuum).
